How big is the business

How to think about this

Revenue tells you scale, not health. The first job is to separate the part of revenue that repeats every year from the part that depends on winning new orders. Then ask what each part is worth on its own. A dollar of service revenue on a 20-year contract is worth more than a dollar of turbine revenue that must be re-won.

Market intuitions
  • The market prices mix, not totals. Two companies with the same revenue trade at different multiples if one is half services.
  • Growth that comes from an acquisition is bought, not earned. Strip it out before you call something 'growth'. GEV's 2026 Electrification jump is mostly Prolec.
  • Look at what is shrinking as hard as what is growing. Onshore Wind falling is a fact the bulls skip.
  • Reported segments are management's story. Product lines are closer to the truth. Always go one level finer than the press release.
Questions a top analyst asks
  1. What share of revenue would still arrive if GEV signed no new orders for two years?
  2. How much of the year-over-year growth is organic, how much is price, how much is acquired?
  3. Which product line is the marginal dollar coming from, and what margin does that line carry?
  4. If I only had the segment table, could I tell this company is in an 'AI supercycle'? If not, why does the stock trade like it is?
  5. What did management stop breaking out this year, and why?

Revenue by quarter: equipment vs services ($B)

Ask yourself
  • Is services growing in dollars, or only holding share while equipment ramps?
  • What would revenue look like with equipment flat? That is the floor.
What it isRevenue is the money GEV bills customers in the quarter. Equipment is new turbines, transformers and grid gear. Services is maintaining the installed fleet: parts, repairs, upgrades.
Why it mattersServices are steadier and carry higher margins. A company with half its revenue in services is less exposed to the boom-and-bust of new orders.
What to watchWhether the services bar keeps growing while equipment ramps. If equipment grows and services stall, the mix gets riskier.

Revenue by segment ($B)

Ask yourself
  • What is Electrification's organic growth once Prolec is removed?
  • Is Wind shrinking by choice or by loss of orders?
What it isGEV runs three segments. Power is gas, nuclear, hydro and steam turbines. Wind is onshore and offshore wind turbines. Electrification is transformers, switchgear, grid software and HVDC.
Why it mattersPower is the profit engine and the AI story. Electrification is the fastest grower after the Prolec transformer deal. Wind loses money.
What to watchThe Electrification bar jumps in 2026 because Prolec was consolidated in February. Compare organic growth, not the reported jump.

Revenue by product line ($B)

Ask yourself
  • Is Gas Power revenue rising because of units, price, or scope such as combined-cycle equipment?
  • Which small lines are being quietly wound down?
What it isThe same revenue cut one level finer, using the product lines GEV reports inside each segment.
Why it mattersThis shows what is actually growing. Gas Power is most of Power. Grid Solutions is most of Electrification. Offshore Wind is small but has produced most of the losses.
What to watchGas Power services versus Gas Power equipment, and whether Onshore Wind keeps shrinking.

Is it making money

How to think about this

Profit has layers. Gross margin is pricing power minus factory cost. Operating margin adds overhead. Net margin adds tax and one-offs. When the three move together the business is changing. When one moves alone, something accounting-shaped happened. Always ask which layer moved and why before you believe a margin number.

Market intuitions
  • Margin expansion during a volume ramp is rare and valuable. It means price is rising faster than cost. The question is how long it lasts.
  • Segment EBITDA is the number the Street models. Get the segment margin bridge right and the rest of the model follows.
  • A loss-making segment that management promises will break even is a bet, not a forecast. Check the arithmetic against the best quarter that segment ever had.
  • One-offs that recur are not one-offs. Restructuring every quarter is a cost of doing business.
  • The multiple is paid on next year's margin, not this year's. Every margin debate is really a 2027 debate.
Questions a top analyst asks
  1. Is gross margin rising because of price, mix, or volume absorbing fixed cost? Each has a different half-life.
  2. What was the margin on the units being built today priced at, and when were those prices set?
  3. If Wind cannot reach the guided loss, how much does that subtract from company EPS, and is it already in the consensus number?
  4. What is the incremental margin, meaning profit change divided by revenue change, over the last four quarters? Is it above or below the segment average?
  5. Which costs are stepping up with the factory expansion, and are they in cost of revenue or in SG&A?
  6. What effective tax rate should I use, and what is the one-off in the reported rate?

Segment EBITDA by quarter ($M)

Ask yourself
  • What does the second half need from Wind for the annual guide to hold, and has Wind ever done that?
  • Is Power's growth in EBITDA faster than its growth in revenue?
What it isEBITDA is profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization. It is the closest thing to cash profit from operations. GEV reports it per segment.
Why it mattersThis is the number analysts model. Power and Electrification make money; Wind loses it every quarter.
What to watchWind must turn positive in the second half of 2026 for the company's guidance to hold. The first half lost $657M.

Segment EBITDA margin (%)

Ask yourself
  • Is Power margin expanding on price, mix or volume, and which of those survives a ramp?
  • What margin do the units ordered in 2024 carry versus those ordered in 2025?
What it isMargin is profit divided by revenue. A 20% margin means 20 cents of every revenue dollar is profit.
Why it mattersRising margin means price and volume are beating cost inflation. Falling margin during a ramp means the factory expansion is costing more than it earns yet.
What to watchPower margin is guided to 17 to 19% for 2026. Whether it keeps expanding in 2027 is the central debate on the stock.

Company-wide margins (%)

Ask yourself
  • Which of the three lines moved this quarter, and was the cause operating or accounting?
  • What is net margin excluding the Prolec revaluation and the tax benefit?
What it isGross margin is revenue minus the direct cost of making the product. Operating margin also subtracts sales, admin and R&D. Net margin is what is left after interest and tax.
Why it mattersThree lines together show where the money goes. A wide gap between gross and operating margin means heavy overhead.
What to watchNet margin spikes in Q4 2025 and Q1 2026 are one-offs: a tax benefit, and the accounting gain from revaluing GEV's old half of Prolec. Ignore them for the model.

Where each revenue dollar goes (%)

Ask yourself
  • Is cost of revenue falling as a share because of price, or because of mix toward services?
  • When does the 1,500-worker hiring wave show up in cost of revenue?
What it isThe cost of revenue, sales and admin, and research and development, each as a share of revenue.
Why it mattersOperating leverage means costs grow slower than revenue, so margins expand. You can see it here directly.
What to watchCost of revenue falling as a share of revenue is the pricing story. Sales and admin should keep shrinking as a share.

Interest, tax and one-offs ($M)

Ask yourself
  • What tax rate belongs in the model, and why does the reported one swing?
  • Is interest income from cash that belongs to customers as deposits?
What it isItems between operating profit and net income: interest cost or income, income tax, restructuring charges, and income from joint ventures.
Why it mattersThese explain why net income and EBITDA move differently. GEV has net cash, so interest is income, not cost.
What to watchThe effective tax rate swings wildly because of one-off tax benefits. Do not use a single quarter's rate in the model.

Cash: what actually arrived

How to think about this

Profit is an opinion. Cash is a fact. But cash has timing. Customer deposits arrive years before the work, so a company in an order boom shows more cash than profit, and a company in an order bust shows less. Always ask: is this cash earned, or borrowed from the future?

Market intuitions
  • Free cash flow far above net income means working capital is helping. Working capital help always reverses; the question is when.
  • Deposits are customer money held in trust for work not yet done. They are a liability with a cash balance attached.
  • The market rewards a cash beat on the day and forgets it in a month if the source was deposits, because everyone can see the reversal coming.
  • Capex guided up is a signal of confidence. Capex delivered below guidance is a signal of caution, or of supplier bottlenecks.
  • Buybacks funded by deposits are buybacks funded by customers. That works until orders slow.
Questions a top analyst asks
  1. What was free cash flow excluding the change in contract liabilities? That is the earned cash.
  2. How many quarters of the current burn rate does the deposit balance cover, and what happens to cash flow when inflow equals burn?
  3. What deposit percentage is implied by deposits divided by new commitments? Is it rising because customers are more desperate, or because GEV asks for more?
  4. Is second-half guidance conservative because management always guides low, or because they see the inflow slowing?
  5. Where did the Prolec cash come from, and what does the balance sheet look like without the deposit tailwind?

Cash from operations, capex and free cash flow ($B)

Ask yourself
  • What is free cash flow excluding the change in deposits?
  • Why is second-half guidance so much lower than the first half?
What it isCash from operations is real cash the business generated. Capex is cash spent on factories and equipment. Free cash flow is the difference, the cash left for shareholders.
Why it mattersProfit is an opinion, cash is a fact. GEV's free cash flow in 2026 has been far above its profit because customers pay deposits up front.
What to watchFirst-half 2026 free cash flow was about $9.9B. Full-year guidance is $11.5 to 12.5B, so the second half is guided to be small.

Cash flow by activity ($B)

Ask yourself
  • How much of financing outflow is buybacks, and is it funded by earned cash or deposits?
  • Was the Prolec purchase price matched by the cash it will generate?
What it isThe three sections of the cash flow statement: operating (the business), investing (factories and acquisitions), financing (debt, buybacks, dividends).
Why it mattersShows how the company uses the cash it makes. In Q1 2026 investing is deeply negative because GEV paid $5.3B for the rest of Prolec.
What to watchWhether financing turns more negative as buybacks grow.

Customer deposits vs backlog ($B)

Ask yourself
  • What deposit rate on new commitments does the balance imply, and is it rising?
  • Under what conditions does this balance shrink, and how fast?
What it isContract liabilities are cash customers paid before GEV delivered, mostly deposits on turbine orders and slot reservations. RPO, remaining performance obligations, is the firm backlog: contracted work not yet delivered.
Why it mattersDeposits are why cash flow is so strong right now. They are also an obligation: GEV must build what it was paid for. The percentage on each bar is deposits as a share of backlog.
What to watchThe ratio rising from 14% to 23% means customers are prepaying a larger slice of each order. That cash reverses only if orders get cancelled.

Customer deposits by segment ($B)

Ask yourself
  • Why is nearly all deposit growth in Power, and what does that say about Electrification's contract terms?
  • Are Wind deposits shrinking because deliveries are happening or because orders stopped?
What it isThe same deposits, split by which segment holds them.
Why it mattersAlmost all of the growth is Power, meaning gas turbine reservations and orders.
What to watchElectrification deposits after Prolec, and whether Wind deposits keep shrinking.

Deposits turned into revenue each quarter ($B)

Ask yourself
  • When do inflow and burn cross, and what is cash flow in that quarter?
  • How much of the burn is Power versus Wind?
What it isEach quarter, some of the deposit balance is recognized as revenue as the work gets done. This is that amount.
Why it mattersCompare it to the deposit inflow. When inflow is far larger than burn, the balance grows and cash flow looks great. When they converge, the cash tailwind fades.
What to watchThe burn rate has been about $3 to 4B per quarter while the balance grew by $8B per quarter in 2026.

The order book

How to think about this

A backlog is a promise, and promises have grades. Firm orders with penalties are the highest grade. Reservations with deposits are lower. Announced projects with no money down are noise. The market tends to price the headline number; the analyst prices the graded number and the speed at which it converts.

Market intuitions
  • Backlog divided by annual capacity is years of visibility. Beyond about four years, more backlog adds little value today and mostly signals pricing power.
  • The market stops rewarding a metric once it has been huge for several quarters. Watch whether the stock still moves on GW announcements.
  • Timing matters more than size. Backlog delivered in 2029 is worth much less than backlog delivered in 2027, and it is exposed to cancellation.
  • Reservation-to-order conversion is the honest demand signal. Signing is free; converting costs money.
  • Compare the peer. If Siemens converts twice as fast, ask why GEV's customers wait longer.
Questions a top analyst asks
  1. What fraction of the '116 GW under contract' has a substantive cancellation penalty?
  2. What is the median age of a reservation before it converts, and is it lengthening?
  3. If capacity is 20 GW a year and backlog plus reservations are 116 GW, what must be true for a 2027 order to matter to 2027 revenue at all?
  4. How much of the equipment backlog is priced at 2024 levels, and how much at 2025 levels?
  5. What happens to the reservation pool if data-center projects slip a year? Which ones are tied to sites with permits and gas supply?
  6. Does the company's definition of backlog match the one the sell-side uses when quoting it?

Backlog by type: equipment vs services ($B)

Ask yourself
  • Has services backlog grown from new contracts or from re-estimating existing ones?
  • What is equipment backlog divided by annual capacity, in years?
What it isRPO split into equipment (turbines and gear to build) and services (long-term maintenance contracts on the installed fleet).
Why it mattersServices backlog is the most valuable half: long, high-margin, hard to cancel. It is also partly an estimate of future work under contracts.
What to watchEquipment backlog has more than doubled in 18 months. Services backlog grows more slowly but is larger in absolute terms.

When the backlog turns into revenue (% within 1, 2, 5 years)

Ask yourself
  • If only 36% of equipment backlog arrives within a year, what 2027 revenue does that imply, and what is consensus?
  • Why is the one-year share falling: longer lead times or later-dated new orders?
What it isGEV states what share of its backlog it expects to deliver within one, two and five years. Cumulative percentages, latest quarter.
Why it mattersA backlog that is delivered later is worth less today, and it means near-term revenue is smaller than the headline suggests.
What to watchThe one-year share of equipment backlog has fallen from 46% to 36% since 2024. The dollar amount within one year still rose, because the total grew faster.

Gas turbine gigawatts per quarter: signed, converted, shipped

Ask yourself
  • Did shipped gigawatts reach 5 in the third quarter? If not, why not, and what does that do to 2027?
  • What share of signed gigawatts are reservations versus firm orders, quarter by quarter?
What it isFrom the earnings press releases. Signed is new commitments, mostly slot reservations. Converted is reservations that became firm orders. Shipped is turbines that left the factory.
Why it mattersThis is the physical pipeline. Signing is easy; shipping is the constraint. GEV says annual output reaches 20 GW from the third quarter of 2026, which means about 5 GW a quarter.
What to watchShipped has been 3 to 5 GW for five quarters. The October 22 release shows whether the step to 5 GW happened.

Gas turbine backlog and slot reservations (GW)

Ask yourself
  • Why are reservations now bigger than firm backlog, and what is the conversion lag?
  • How many gigawatts of reservations belong to customers without a site, a permit, or gas supply?
What it isBacklog is firm gas turbine orders in gigawatts. Slot reservations are deposits that hold a place in the production line but are not yet firm orders.
Why it mattersTogether they are the '116 GW under contract' headline. Only the backlog is in RPO.
What to watchReservations are now larger than firm backlog. How fast they convert, and whether any lapse, decides how real the headline is.

Quality signals

How to think about this

Quality means: will these profits hold. The clues are in the footnotes, not the headlines. Estimate changes, warranty reserves, and inventory turns tell you whether the company is over-earning today at the expense of tomorrow. Read the footnote every quarter and chart it. Nobody else does.

Market intuitions
  • A negative revision to contract profit estimates is management admitting yesterday's profit was too high. A pattern of them is a trend, not noise.
  • Warranty reserves that lag a product ramp are a future charge. New models fail more in their first years.
  • Inventory rising faster than revenue is either pre-building for a ramp, which is good, or unsold product, which is bad. The company will call it the first. Check shipments.
  • Restructuring that never ends is a margin cost the adjusted numbers hide.
  • The best short ideas in industrials come from the quality section, not the revenue section.
Questions a top analyst asks
  1. What is the cumulative profit revision on service contracts over the last eight quarters, and what share of service backlog does it represent?
  2. What drove the revision: cost inflation, parts availability, fleet running harder than assumed, or contract renegotiation?
  3. Is warranty accrual per dollar of equipment revenue rising as new turbine models ramp?
  4. How many days of revenue is inventory, and how does that compare with the peer set?
  5. Which adjusted-earnings exclusions are recurring, and what is EPS without them?

Service-contract profit revisions ($M per quarter)

Ask yourself
  • What is the nine-month revision in the Q3 10-Q, and did management explain it?
  • Is the revision concentrated in one fleet or contract type, for example HA turbines under fixed-price service agreements?
What it isGEV estimates the lifetime profit of each long-term service agreement. When it changes the estimate, the difference hits that quarter's revenue. Negative means it now expects less profit on existing contracts.
Why it mattersThis is the quality signal on the services half of the business. It sits in a footnote nobody quotes.
What to watchFirst-half 2026 was about minus $218M, five times the first half of 2025. The nine-month number arrives around October 22.

Warranty reserve ($B) and as % of quarterly revenue

Ask yourself
  • Is the reserve per dollar of equipment revenue rising as new models ship?
  • What is the claims-paid trend versus reserve additions?
What it isThe warranty reserve is money set aside for expected repairs on products already sold.
Why it mattersA reserve rising faster than revenue means quality problems or new products with unknown failure rates. Flat means the ramp is not hurting quality yet.
What to watchThe line, reserve as a share of revenue, is the one to watch during the factory ramp.

Inventory, receivables and contract assets ($B)

Ask yourself
  • Is inventory growth explained by the Q3 shipment plan, or is it building faster than shipments?
  • Are receivables growing faster than revenue, meaning customers are paying slower?
What it isInventory is materials and unfinished turbines. Receivables is money customers owe. Contract assets is work done but not yet billable under the contract terms.
Why it mattersWorking capital is cash tied up in running the business. Inventory rising with revenue is normal; rising faster than revenue means slower turns or pre-building.
What to watchInventory has grown from about $9B to almost $13B as production ramps.

Restructuring charges ($M)

Ask yourself
  • What was excluded from adjusted EPS in the last four quarters, and does it add up to a recurring cost?
What it isOne-off costs of closing sites, cutting jobs or exiting businesses.
Why it mattersLarge or repeated charges mean the 'one-off' is really recurring. Small and shrinking is healthy.
What to watchCharges have shrunk to near zero in 2026.

Balance sheet and shareholders

How to think about this

The balance sheet is where past decisions live. Goodwill is the premium paid for acquisitions. Debt is a claim ahead of shareholders. Buybacks are management's opinion of the share price, backed with cash. Read all three together: a company buying back stock at 35 times earnings while carrying fresh acquisition goodwill is making two bets at once.

Market intuitions
  • Net cash gives optionality but earns nothing. The market values what the cash will do, not the cash itself.
  • Goodwill is only a problem when it is written down. It is written down when the acquisition misses. Watch Prolec's organic growth.
  • Buybacks lift EPS mechanically. Separate EPS growth from profit growth before you praise it.
  • Liabilities that grow because of deposits are not leverage. Analysts who compute debt-to-equity without adjusting get GEV wrong.
  • Share count falling while the stock rises means management is paying more for each share retired. Ask if they would buy at this price with their own money.
Questions a top analyst asks
  1. How much EPS growth in the last year came from a lower share count versus higher profit?
  2. At what share price does the buyback stop making sense against reinvesting in capacity?
  3. What return did GEV pay for Prolec, and what must Prolec earn for that goodwill to hold?
  4. What is the true net cash after subtracting deposits that will be worked off within a year?
  5. What is the dilution from stock awards each year, and does the buyback merely offset it?

Assets, liabilities and equity ($B)

Ask yourself
  • What is net cash after subtracting deposits due within a year?
  • Why did GEV issue bonds while holding net cash?
What it isTotal assets are everything the company owns. Total liabilities are what it owes, including customer deposits. Equity is the difference, the owners' stake.
Why it mattersGEV's liabilities grow with deposits, which is not debt. Actual borrowing is small.
What to watchDebt rose to about $2.9B in 2026 after a bond issue. Cash is larger than debt.

Goodwill and intangibles ($B)

Ask yourself
  • What organic growth must Prolec deliver to justify $9.7B of purchase price?
  • How much of reported profit decline is amortization that EBITDA ignores?
What it isWhen a company buys another for more than the value of its physical assets, the excess is recorded as goodwill and intangibles. Intangibles are amortized, meaning expensed over years.
Why it mattersThe jump in Q1 2026 is the Prolec purchase. Amortization of Prolec intangibles is now about $180 to 240M per quarter of non-cash expense that lowers reported profit but not EBITDA.
What to watchAny future write-down of goodwill would signal the acquisition underperformed.

Buybacks and dividends ($B)

Ask yourself
  • How much EPS growth is share count versus profit?
  • Would management buy at this price with their own money? Check insider purchases.
What it isCash returned to shareholders by buying back shares or paying dividends.
Why it mattersBuybacks reduce the share count, which lifts earnings per share. GEV has been buying back more each quarter.
What to watchWhether buybacks continue at $2B+ per quarter once the deposit cash tailwind fades.

Diluted earnings per share ($)

Ask yourself
  • What is EPS excluding one-offs, and how does the forward multiple look on that number?
  • How much of next year's EPS growth is already in the deposit-funded buyback?
What it isNet income divided by the number of shares. Diluted means it includes shares that could be created by employee stock awards.
Why it mattersThis is the number the stock price is compared with. Forward P/E of about 35 means the price is 35 times next year's expected EPS.
What to watchThe Q1 2026 figure includes the Prolec revaluation gain and is not repeatable.

The research corpus: what we built and what it found

Everything above came from GE Vernova's own filings. This section is the wider research corpus the team built: 34 companies' filings, competitor and customer reports, grid-operator studies, government generator data, academic papers and dated commentary, stored in one 4 GB database and read by local models. First what it contains, then what it found.

How to think about this

A corpus is not a thesis. It is a place where a thesis can be tested cheaply. The way to use it: start from something the market believes, write the sentence down, then look for the table or filing that would prove it wrong. Most beliefs survive. The few that do not are the memo.

Research intuitions
  • Primary sources beat commentary. When a news story and a 10-Q disagree, the 10-Q wins and the story tells you what the crowd thinks.
  • Series beat snapshots. One footnote number across ten quarters is worth more than ten numbers from one quarter.
  • Joins beat reading. The findings came from putting two tables next to each other, not from reading either one.
  • Verification kills half of everything. Of the sweep's findings, about half were reproduced and not refuted. The refuted half is still useful as a list of traps.
  • Absence is information. No filing gives the deposit terms. That gap is itself the most important fact about the reservations debate.
Questions to ask of the corpus
  1. Which of these findings changes a number in the model, and by how much?
  2. For each finding, what is the single check on October 22 that confirms or kills it?
  3. Which findings point the same direction, and is that direction the one the team wants, or the one the data wants?
  4. What would a Citadel analyst with expert calls know that this corpus cannot tell us, and how do we hedge that gap?
  5. Which dead ends should we stop spending time on?

Findings board from the multi-agent sweep

Twelve finder agents searched the corpus and the web with different lenses; each finding was re-run by a second agent and attacked by a third. Green survived both. Orange was not re-checked. Red reproduced but the conclusion failed.

The technical research: arXiv, IEEE and the physics

Three multi-agent runs searched for a mispricing: a broad corpus sweep, a wedge-selection tournament, and this one, a technical sweep across arXiv, IEEE, OpenAlex and the corpus academic tier. Sixteen research lenses read 212 papers and produced 38 findings. Every finding was then attacked by a physics skeptic who re-derived the central number from a second source, and independently re-priced by a quantifier who rebuilt the dollars-per-share arithmetic from scratch. Zero findings survived both checks. That is the result, and it is worth more than a weak yes: it says the debate about this stock is not a hidden technical fact, it is the multiple. What follows is the complete record, including the nine popular bear arguments the physics killed.

Result: no technical wedge.

Every finding had to clear four bars: a quantified physical fact from a citable paper; a mechanism reaching a named GEV financial line; materiality in dollars per share (EBITDA impact x 25 multiple / 266.3M shares, against the $940.33 reference price); and a testable prediction with a date and a kill condition. Anything worth under about $10 a share, roughly 1%, is not a wedge no matter how elegant the physics.

The research effort

The one piece of physics that matters

GE's own maintenance manual sets two clocks on a turbine: fired hours and starts. Whichever fills first triggers an expensive inspection. Divide the two limits and you get 34.7 hours per start. A machine that runs long shifts is limited by hours. A machine that starts and stops all day is limited by starts, and needs an overhaul far sooner than an hours-based cost model expects. New peakers sit well left of the line. The installed fleet sits well right of it.

The fleet is younger than the story assumes

This is disclosed-number arithmetic with no assumption chain, and it is the strongest defensible claim in the file, in either direction. It also explains why services earn about $15M per gigawatt-year today against a $25M target, with no need for any AI or duty-cycle story at all.

The newer machine is tighter on starts

The number that breaks the AI framing

Service-contract profit estimates are being cut, and that is real. But fiscal 2024 ran at more than double the fiscal 2025 rate, at a time when essentially no data-center-linked H-class capacity was operating. A judge holding the FY24 filing ends an 'AI duty cycles are eating the annuity' pitch with one question.

Everything, priced

Each bar is an independent re-derivation of what the finding is worth per share, not the researcher's own estimate. The dotted line is a 20% move. Nothing comes close.

How the findings scored themselves

The physics that survived, and the question that decides it

The starts-versus-hours crossover is real, and the fleet is on the safe side of it

GER-3620 Rev P sets the 7HA.02 hot-gas-path inspection at 25,000 factored fired hours or 720 factored starts, whichever comes first. Divide and the crossover is 34.7 fired hours per start. New simple-cycle peakers run 4-8 hours per start, five times below it, so starts would govern. But the installed HA fleet runs 147 hours per start (3.0M hours / 20,400 starts), 4.2x clear on the hours side. The fleet that generates services revenue today is hours-limited, not starts-limited.

The average HA turbine has not reached its first major overhaul

The fleet averages 28,571 operating hours per unit (3.6M hours / 126 units, FY25 10-K) against a 50,000-hour major inspection. At the measured ~6,000 hours/year run rate the first major arrives in about 3.6 years. This single disclosed fact explains the gap between management's $25M/GW-year services target and today's realised ~$15M with zero duty-cycle content. It is a tailwind, not a headwind.

The services accounting breaks the duty-cycle chain anyway

GEV recognises service-contract revenue on cost-to-cost percentage of completion, and the FY25 10-K says billing happens “per hour of usage and upon the occurrence of a major maintenance event.” Several researchers quoted only the first half. A harsher duty cycle that pulls maintenance forward pulls billings forward with it, so the sign may be positive.

Nobody could establish how the contracts actually bill

Neither the researchers nor the skeptics could determine from public sources whether GEV's service agreements bill on actual or factored fired hours. If factored, GE's own severity formula already prices duty cycle and the effect is zero. This one question flips the sign on roughly a third of the technical work and is the highest-value thing to ask investor relations.

Nine arguments the physics killed

This is the most useful part of the section. Each of these is an intuitive bear argument that other teams may pitch, and each is contradicted by a hard number.

Part-load operation wears turbines faster

GE's own GER-3620 Rev P sets the hours-based load severity factor at 1.0 all the way down to base load, and in combined-cycle mode firing temperature does not drop until below ~80% of rated output. Part-load start cycles below 60% carry a factor of 0.5 and therefore extend the interval.

Never say this on stage. It is the most intuitive bear argument and it is false.

Batteries are eating the peaker market

Operating US battery capacity went from 8.9 GW to 53.3 GW (+499%) between January 2023 and July 2026, while simple-cycle gas utilization went up. PJM accredits a 4-hour battery below a simple-cycle peaker for capacity value.

Storage contests energy, not firm capacity. The GW are not at risk.

Reciprocating engines are taking turbine share

Planned US reciprocating-engine capacity is flat at ~1.0 GW while planned turbine capacity went from 11.3 GW to 44.1 GW. Recip share of planned gas collapsed from ~8% to 2.2%.

The bridge-power narrative is real but tiny in the data.

Hydrogen blending changes the economics

EIA's planned-generator file contains exactly one hydrogen unit nationally, 50 MW, and it is a fusion pilot that has been miscoded.

Hydrogen optionality in a US-driven story is worth approximately zero.

Liquid cooling shrinks the power that was contracted

Uptime Institute puts industry average PUE at 1.52, flat for seven years. Campuses sanctioned in 2026 are designed at 1.1-1.25 and the contract embeds that number, not a survey mean of a legacy fleet. Rack density rising 135 to 230 to 600 kW swamps the gain.

Priced at $76/share by the researcher; correctly scoped it is under $4.

AI needs less power than people think, so orders fall

GEV has 116 GW under contract against 20 GW/yr of output rising to 30 GW/yr by 2030, roughly five years oversubscribed in an industry-wide shortage. Equipment revenue is recognized over time on costs incurred against contracts already signed.

Demand haircuts trim the back of the queue, not this year's revenue. Every efficiency-driven bear thesis dies here.

Grid-enhancing technologies displace new gas

FERC excluded dynamic line ratings from Order 2023's alternative-technologies list; reconductoring programs run on a 2035 horizon.

Cannot touch a 3-12 month thesis.

The SMR option is a big part of the story

Four independent sources put realized BWRX-300 capex at US$12,530-17,949/kW, which is 2.5-3.6x the ~$5,000/kWe viability threshold in the published literature. Total nuclear/SMR option value bounds at $15-32/share (1.6-3.4%).

Real, small, and far out of the money. The licensing leg is de-risking, which kills the obvious bear catalyst too.

The corpus academic tier holds the AI-hardware answer

It is a power-systems and wind library. Zero hits for “energy per token”, “roofline”, “arithmetic intensity” or “factored fired hours”. The signal sits in 42 arXiv data-center papers from 2025-26, which were genuinely unmined.

Go to arXiv directly; do not mine the corpus for chip physics.

  • short Because Section 232 now taxes the article and not the metal, a US-built transformer carries a 12-21 point structural cost advantage over an identical imported one — and Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy and Eaton's new US plants start producing in 2027, exactly when GEV's import channel is scaling and the 15% band expires
    Section 232 reaches imports, not domestic manufacture. A transformer BUILT in the US pays duty only on its imported inputs: GOES at 50% under Annex I-A on ~$129k of core steel in a representative 100 MVA unit, plus copper, against a ~$3.5M selling price — an effective ~3-4% of article value. The decision: what the Street expects, and which side to take

Two further runs closed the research out: a 31-agent sweep of everything that is not a filing (what the Street expects, who owns the stock, what the bonds say, what suppliers say, what regulators are doing), and a 54-agent run that built the strongest possible long case and the strongest possible short case from sixteen independent angles, attacked every one twice, and put the survivors to a five-judge panel. 268 agents across five runs.

LONG, defensively.

Decision: LONG — defensive, modest target, both sides weak. All sixteen cases were killed, but they died differently, and that asymmetry is the decision. The eight shorts died because their mechanisms were wrong. The eight longs died because they were already priced. “Your facts don't hold” is a worse verdict than “your facts hold but everyone knows them”: you can defend the second in a question-and-answer room. Panel voted 4 to 1 long on a forced choice.

Read this before using the headline argument

The strongest available argument is a hypothesis, not a finding. The rebuttal to the one published Sell note — that percentage-of-completion accounting already ran the cheap 2024 order vintage through 2025 and 2026 earnings — has a real flaw. Percentage-of-completion fixes the margin rate when the contract is signed and changes when margin is recognised, not how much. A turbine sold cheaply in 2024 recognises its thin margin across whatever years it is built in. The rebuttal only holds if those 2024 contracts are largely complete by the end of 2026, and nobody established that. The analyst who wrote the Sell note covers this company professionally and knows the accounting. Establish the completion share from the filings before this goes anywhere near a memo.

What the stock actually costs

Correcting the market multiple changes the whole valuation argument. GEV is priced at roughly twice the S&P 500, not 1.6 times.

Sixteen cases, sixteen deaths

The margin record

The published Sell note argues 2027 ships at about three points of equipment margin. GEV has already printed 10.4% for a full year and 13.1% in a quarter.

Cash, with the deposits taken out

This is the strongest argument against the long and it survived every attack. It belongs in the risk section, stated plainly.

How every case died

The eight long cases — already priced

  • Fleet services wave — 70% of it is just unit growth; the differentiated piece is ~$6/share and lands in 2028
  • Deposit engine — Values a customer liability at 100 cents as equity; the market marked the July cash-flow raise DOWN 8.7%
  • Backlog conversion — Model collapses to one input; the same method a year earlier claimed 98% visibility against 66-70% realised
  • Vintage rebuttal — Mechanism excellent, but its 44.5% drop-through contradicts its own build (31.2%) and the 10-K's 22.5%
  • Electrification — Compares GEV on 2028 estimates to peers on FY25 actuals; 43% of segment EBITDA cannot offset a Power de-rate
  • De-rating mispricing — Capitalises the price decline itself; the drawdown was a sector move (Vertiv -25.5%, Quanta -11.6%)
  • Capacity execution — The 400 installed machines are a company press release; 5.2 GW was already printed in Q2'25
  • Demand durability — Defends 2.6% of market cap against a duration problem

The eight short cases — wrong mechanisms

  • Conversion gap — A denominator artifact. GEV converted 10 GW against Siemens' 12
  • Services quality — Divides a net backlog change by GW, ignoring $6.6B of run-off
  • Wind bridge — The miss is real ($480M) but sits inside the guided band with ~$560M of cushion; the market paid +13.75% on the worst Wind quarter in two years
  • Margin vintage — Dies to percentage-of-completion, and 82% of it was an unsourced multiple assertion
  • Multiple compression — Mixes guidance vintages; the “never raised” claim is false ($14B→$22B→$24B in 13 months)
  • Share loss — Assumes a demand-constrained market in a franchise sold out to 2031
  • Cash normalisation — Right observation, wrong forward model; the liquidation ratio double-counts deposits carrying no backlog
  • Shipment stall — Its trigger metric correlates -0.31 with the revenue line it is supposed to drive

What kills the thesis

All four land at Q3 earnings on October 28, which falls after the October 22-24 finals. Say that from the podium rather than letting a judge point it out.

Q3 equipment gross margin below 9.0%

FY25 was 10.39%, Q2'26 was 13.10%. Two consecutive quarters below 9% and the margin pillar is dead; flip to short.

Q3 Power segment EBITDA margin below 17.0%

The floor of management's own guide, in the quarter the volume ramp is supposed to land.

Q3 gas turbine gigawatts below 4.5 with HA units at 4 or fewer

Management committed to 5 GW a quarter from Q3'26. Ten straight quarters have printed 3 to 5, with nothing above 5.2.

January 2027: 2026 backlog margin change below +4 points

2025 printed +6 points and “at least $8B”. Management committed on Sep 16 to disclose it. This is the direct scorecard.

The question you have to answer on stage

The red teams' killer question

At $940 you are paying 21.4 times management's own 2028 EBITDA target. Capitalise a perfectly delivered 2028 at the 25 times you say is fair, discount it two years, and you get $877 — below where the stock trades today. That plan needs Power at 22% and Electrification at 22%, and neither segment has ever printed above 18.9% or 18.6% in any quarter, while Wind has had exactly one non-negative quarter in its history. So what am I being paid for the execution risk?

The answer: nothing on 2028 — which is why the target is +12% and not +25%, and why we sit below the Street. You are paid for the next twelve months, in which the three arguments that took $256 off this stock each fail again on the record.

The other side's best argument

Put this in the risk section. Do not dodge it.

Earned free cash flow is approximately zero, and the market is calling it a 4.8% yield. First-half operating cash flow of $10,680M contains a $14,087M increase in customer deposits, so operating cash excluding deposits was -$3,407M. FY25 was -$3,363M on the same basis. Since the spin, cumulative free cash flow of $15.3B sits on a $24.5B deposit build while $7.6B went back to shareholders. Deposits of $40,037M are 3.05x cash on hand and 3.35x book equity. And 40% of the annual bonus plus 50% of the long-term plan pay on this line, with no orders or backlog metric as a counterweight. This survived every attack. It is the question a judge will ask. Concede the quality point; reject the cliff — the deposits are non-refundable and are discharged by delivering turbines at a positive margin, not by wiring cash back.
